summary:
Light&Link is an interactive 3D web application that helps mission planners, educators, and the public rapidly evaluate lunar south pole landing sites by visualizing co-visibility windows —the periods when a lander receives direct sunlight for solar power while maintaining an unobstructed line of sight to Earth for direct communication.

Combining high-resolution topographic data from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) with Sun and Earth ephemeris vectors from JPL Horizons, Light&Link renders local 3D lunar terrain in Three.js with real-time solar shadows, slope hazard maps, and a dynamic laser link to Earth. Clicking anywhere on the terrain instantly recalculates the surrounding 360-degree horizon mask in the browser, showing how small location or schedule shifts affect mission survival.

To address both engineering and outreach needs, the platform offers two experiences powered by the same physical model: Mission Planner Mode, where teams compare sites and launch dates side-by-side, inspect battery telemetry, and export CSV/JSON reports; and Explorer Mode, where an astronaut guide named Alba leads users through six interactive missions. By turning complex orbital geometry into an accessible visual sandbox, Light&Link accelerates early mission trade-off decisions and brings lunar exploration challenges to everyone.
details:
Light&Link

What does it do and how does it work?

Light&Link is an interactive 3D web application designed to evaluate landing site viability near the lunar south pole by solving a critical mission-planning question: Where and when can a lunar lander receive direct sunlight for power while simultaneously maintaining a direct line of sight to Earth for communication?

To achieve smooth, real-time performance in a standard web browser without polar distortion or heavy 3D lag, our architecture separates physical data preparation from 3D rendering:

  • Physics & Horizon Engine: Python scripts pre-process high-resolution topographic elevation maps from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) alongside Sun and Earth positions from NASA’s JPL Horizons System. For any landing coordinate, the system builds a full 360-degree local Horizon Mask (measured every tenth of a degree) that accounts for surrounding craters, ridges, and the Moon's lack of atmosphere.
  • Real-Time Co-Visibility Evaluation: The web app compares the Sun's and Earth's angles in the sky against the local terrain height in milliseconds across multi-week lunar timelines. Whenever both the Sun and Earth clear the surrounding mountain ridges at the same time, the system flags an active Co-Visibility Window.
  • Interactive 3D Terrain & Dynamic Relocation: Using Three.js and WebGL 2, Light&Link renders local 20-by-20-kilometer lunar terrain patches deformed from 16-bit LOLA heightmaps, surrounded by a lower-detail outer horizon ring. Directional solar lighting casts dynamic shadows matching the exact solar position, while an articulated CLPS-style lander tracks Earth with a laser beam that shifts from emerald green (clear signal) to red (blocked by a ridge). Users can click anywhere on the terrain to relocate the lander, triggering an instant in-browser recalculation of its 360-degree horizon, battery charge cycles, and communication windows.

What benefits does it have?

  • Rapid Scenario & Delay Evaluation: Traditional tools like Quickmap, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons require navigating separate technical interfaces and interpreting raw data tables. Light&Link consolidates elevation, illumination, slope hazards, and communication geometry into a single interactive view, allowing users to compare alternative sites or delayed launch windows in seconds.
  • Dual-Mode Accessibility: Rather than forcing non-specialists into complex telemetry or limiting engineers to simplified visuals, Light&Link powers two distinct experiences from the exact same terrain model:
    • Explorer Mode (Gamified Story): An astronaut guide named Alba leads students and the public through six interactive missions—starting on a dangerous steep slope, relocating the lander to flatter terrain, hunting for an eight-hour continuous co-visibility window to run a simulated experiment, and comparing candidate sites.
    • Mission Planner Mode (Technical Suite): Provides engineering and science teams with side-by-side site and date comparisons, 360-degree elevation charts, terrain slope hazard maps (highlighting safe flat ground versus steep tip-over risks), simulated battery and thermal telemetry, and one-click CSV or JSON data exports.
  • Zero Specialized Hardware Required: By serving lightweight JSON payloads and 16-bit PNG heightmaps, the platform runs smoothly in any modern WebGL 2-compatible browser without specialized workstations.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Light&Link bridges the gap between planetary mission planning and public STEM outreach. For mission planners, science teams, and educators, it provides an agile sandbox to rapidly visualize why moving a lander just a few hundred meters along a crater rim—or shifting a launch date by two weeks—can dramatically alter mission survival and scientific return. For students and the general public, it turns abstract orbital mechanics (such as Earth's wobble, low grazing polar sunlight, and permanently shadowed craters) into tangible cause-and-effect decisions, inspiring deeper engagement with NASA’s Artemis and Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) exploration goals.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Frontend & 3D Graphics: TypeScript, HTML5, CSS3, Three.js, WebGL 2, and Vite.
  • Backend & Infrastructure: Node.js, Fastify, PostgreSQL (for storing and sharing team mission scenarios), and Redis (for fast caching).
  • Data Processing & NASA Datasets: Python scripts for preparing NASA LOLA elevation data, JPL Horizons ephemeris tables, and surface textures from the NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit.
  • AI & Media Production Tools: OpenAI Codex and Gemini for development acceleration and prototyping, ImageGen for visual illustrations, and HeyGen for Alba’s voice narration and background music.
  • Hardware: Standard developer laptops running Windows and Linux environments with consumer GPUs for local browser testing.

How is your project creative?

  • Turning Telemetry into Interactive Storytelling: Instead of presenting static charts or a passive 3D viewer, we built an interactive story loop where learners actively rescue a mission—experiencing firsthand why steep crater walls block Earth signals and drain lander batteries.
  • Instant In-Browser Horizon Recalculation: By keeping the 16-bit elevation grid in client memory, clicking a new landing spot on the 3D surface dynamically recalculates a full 360-degree horizon profile in milliseconds, immediately updating both the 3D laser obstruction physics and the multi-week mission timeline.
  • Visualizing Invisible Constraints: Features like the Slope Hazard Overlay, Orbital Sky Paths (showing the Sun’s low grazing arc and Earth’s figure-eight wobble path), and real-time Direct-to-Earth laser collision detection make invisible geometric trade-offs immediately obvious to any observer.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Engineering & Physical Trade-offs: We incorporated real operational constraints including landing tilt thresholds (flagging slopes steeper than 15 degrees), observer and antenna height above the lunar regolith (such as 2 meters versus 10 meters), and the absence of atmospheric light bending on the Moon.
  • Polar Distortion & Performance: Standard spherical 3D globes suffer from severe distortion near the south pole and lag when rendering multi-gigabyte elevation maps. We solved this by projecting local flat-grid terrain patches paired with an outer Level-of-Detail ring and pre-computed horizon lookup tables.
  • Scientific Transparency & Accessibility: We explicitly display data sources (LOLA and JPL Horizons) inside the interface, clarify where models are illustrative (such as the simplified battery curve and geometric line-of-sight approximation), and support keyboard controls alongside clear on-screen dialogue for Alba’s narration.
